approved: Australian Workforce and Productivity Agency Repeal Bill 2014
Written by a model from the explanatory memorandum; not the record
This bill would abolish the Australian Workforce and Productivity Agency.
It would repeal the Australian Workforce and Productivity Agency Act 2008.
The agency's advisory functions would move to the Department of Industry.
Repeals the Australian Workforce and Productivity Agency Act 2008.
Abolishes the Australian Workforce and Productivity Agency.
Transfers the agency's functions to the Department of Industry.
The Australian Workforce and Productivity Agency and the Department of Industry.

Sue Lines I move the second reading amendment standing in the name of Senator Carr: At the end of the motion, add "but the Senate notes that the Government has failed to guarantee that the critical independent research to Government and industry in relation to Australia's current, emerging and future skills and workforce development needs will continue to be carried out and made public". The Australian Workforce and Productivity Agency is one of those interesting agencies for which there does not seem to be solid reason to abolish it. We are somewhat perplexed as to why the government would abolish an agency which, for all intents and purposes, is doing a really good job. Amazingly, on 9 June—and perhaps all the arms of government were not speaking to one another—the Hon. Andrew Robb and Senator the Hon. Michaelia Cash put out a media release in which they talked about the Skilled Occupations List and referred to the great work that the Australian Workforce and Productivity Agency does in providing annual recommendations on the Skilled Occupations List. Minister Robb went on to say: The AWPA analyses evidence such as the labour market, education and training, migration and general economic and demographic data to make sure we get the balance right. So perhaps whoever made the wise decision to abolish this agency had not told either Minister Robb or Senator Cash because as late as 9 June they were certainly extolling the virtues and the values of the Australian Workforce and Productivity Agency. Indeed, earlier this year, during the TAFE Senate inquiry, we heard surprise at this decision from Senator O'Sullivan. At the conclusion of the evidence given by the Australian Workforce and Productivity Agency, Mr Robin Shreeve, the CEO, told us that it was to be abolished. I asked Mr Shreeve: Finally, can you tell us what is happening to your board? Mr Shreeve said: We anticipate that from 1 July the functions of AWPA will be folded into the Department of Industry. I asked:
Stephen Parry The question now is that the motion, as amended, be agreed to.

Moved the second reading of the Australian Workforce and Productivity Agency Repeal Bill, explaining that the agency's staff and functions will transfer to the Department of Industry, and thanked current and former board members for their contribution to skills policy.

Opposed abolishing the Australian Workforce and Productivity Agency, moving an amendment to preserve its independent research function, and noted Labor had invested more than $19 billion in skills and training while in government.

Opposed abolishing AWPA, saying Queensland lost 11,700 jobs in the latest month bringing unemployment to 6.1 per cent, and that budget cuts to family payments would leave some families in the electorate around $6,000 a year worse off.

Defended abolishing AWPA as part of streamlining government, citing a 100 per cent increase in public servant credit card spending over four years and the NBN's $6.5 billion spent to reach just 3 per cent of the population under Labor.

Opposed abolishing AWPA, citing over 28,000 announced job losses across Australia's 30 largest employers, including 5,000 at Qantas and more than 6,000 in automotive manufacturing, and quoted academic Leesa Wheelahan questioning where independent skills advice would now come from.

Argued that scrapping the Australian Workforce and Productivity Agency removes independent advice needed for workforce planning, moved an amendment calling on the government to guarantee continued public advice on skills and productivity, and criticised a $30 billion cut to schools alongside other education cuts.

Argued that abolishing the Australian Workforce and Productivity Agency removes unnecessary duplication by folding its functions into the Department of Industry, and cited Labor's $123 billion in deficits and an interest bill of $1,000 million a month as reasons for the reform.

Answered that transferring the Australian Workforce and Productivity Agency's staff and functions into the Department of Industry would strengthen direct engagement with employers, defended the government's consultation process including a 3 April COAG announcement, and rejected the opposition's amendment to guarantee continued independent advice.
